title: Microburst Token Economy and Soft Isolation PRD - rough
body:
Context and motivation:
We frequently see workloads that are mostly steady with occasional short spikes (microbursts) that are extremely latency-sensitive. Dedicated customers want predictable baseline capacity but also the ability to handle transient spikes without opening up expensive reserved capacity or impacting neighbors. Current approaches (static burst credits, simple quota-based throttles) trade either cost or customer experience.

Goal (what success looks like):
- Customers keep baseline reserved throughput for steady traffic while being able to absorb short spikes up to X tokens/sec with minimal 99th percentile tail increase.
- Platform avoids cascading preemptions and noisy-neighbor failures when many tenants spike simultaneously.
- Autoscaling remains cost-effective: platform-level spend increases only for sustained load, not short microbursts.
- Operators get actionable observability: headroom, per-tenant credit balance, eviction likelihood.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or for very large, sustained bursts (>5 minutes).
- Not addressing model-specific degradation (quantization fallbacks) in this doc.

High-level proposal: Microburst Token Economy + Soft-Isolation Throttler
- Each tenant gets a baseline reservation (existing).
- In addition, assign a microburst token bucket (MTB) with configurable parameters: refill-rate (tokens/minute), burst-capacity (max tokens), TTL for tokens (prevents hoarding). Tokens represent short extra compute headroom (proxy for concurrent slots, or GPU allocation units).
- When a request exceeds baseline capacity, the serving control plane consumes MTB tokens instead of instantly rejecting or forcing a model fallback. Token consumption maps to a short-duration elevated slot allocation or fast-path CPU/GPU credit.
- If MTB drained, requests are routed to defined fallback policies: queue with soft-degradation, model-fallback (cheaper/quantized), or rate-limit depending on tenant tier.
- Soft Isolation: dynamic per-tenant throttle that uses token balances and local congestion signals (latency, queue depth, GPU utilization) to gently shape traffic rather than hard-cut preemption. Implemented as a hierarchical leaky bucket with tenancy-aware weights.

Why this helps:
- Enables controlled, measurable short bursts without forcing autoscaler churn.
- Limits blast radius: token exhaustion causes graceful fallback instead of noisy eviction.
- Provides clear knobs for sales/CS to offer burst packages (e.g., X microburst tokens/day).

Key design components:
1) Token accounting service (centralized ledger, sharded per-pool)
   - API: allocate_tokens(tenant, amount, ttl), consume(tenant, amount), observe(tenant)
   - Needs low-latency reads during admission checks; strongly consistent for consumption to avoid double-spend. Consider a fast in-cluster store (etcd shim / in-memory sharded cache with reconciliation).

2) Admission and routing layer changes (Serving control plane)
   - Admission controller reads token balance + local pool capacity. If pool has spare slots and tenant has tokens -> allow fast-path. If tokens available but pool constrained -> enqueue with token reservation (ticket).
   - Fallback mapping: per-tenant policy order: 1) fast-path (tokens) 2) queue (with SLA window) 3) model-fallback 4) rate-limit.

3) Soft-isolation engine (per-worker shaping)
   - Implement per-tenant shaping queues that adjust egress concurrency based on measured latency gradients and token balance.
   - Use additive-increase/multiplicative-decrease style control: increase concurrency slowly when tail latency stable, cut aggressively on tail spikes.

4) Autoscaler interaction
   - Autoscaler sees effective inflight demand including token-driven fast-paths. But we add hysteresis: requests covered by tokens are marked transient so autoscaler ignores them for short window (configurable) unless sustained beyond threshold.
   - Add a sustained-burst metric (e.g., > 3min above threshold) to trigger scale-up.

Economic model & productization ideas:
- Default MTB for tiers: Developer (50 tokens/min, cap 500/day), Business (200 tokens/min, cap 5k/day), Enterprise (custom).
- Tokens as a billable add-on (monthly pool or refill rate), or as part of reserved capacity bundles.
- CS playbook: offer burst credits during onboarding for high-variability customers.

Operational runbook (initial):
- Stage 0: Simulation and offline capacity planner. Run a 30-day backtest on customer telemetry to compute expected token usage and hit rates.
- Stage 1: Canary in a single region on non-critical pools with 3 tenants owned by solutions-eng. Monitor 99p latency, token spend, and tail-error rate.
- Stage 2: Expand to beta customers with opt-in.

Observability & SLOs to add:
- Per-tenant: token_balance, tokens_consumed/day, token_hit_rate (fraction of burst requests served by tokens), fallback_rate, enqueue_time_p50/90/99.
- Pool-level: headroom_ratio, fast-path_inflight, queue_depth, preemption_events.
- Platform: token-led-cost_delta (estimated extra GPU-minutes due to tokens), fraction-of-tenants-using-burst > 10%.
- SLOs: 99p latency increase due to microbursts < 15% for paid-tier tenants when tokens available.

Prototype decisions / technical tradeoffs:
- Consistency vs latency for token ledger: strongly consistent prevents double-spend but adds round trips; eventual-consistent cache with periodic reconciliation might be acceptable if admission logic pessimistically locks on consume. Start with strongly consistent for canary.
- Location of enforcement: centralized vs per-worker. Centralized simplifies accounting but adds latency; per-worker caches can be fast but risk staleness. Hybrid: central master ledger + local LRU caches with short TTL and optimistic consumption + server-side reconciliation.
- Autoscaler hysteresis values (example): ignore token-covered surges shorter than 3 minutes, escalate if > 6 minutes sustained. Tuned by canary data.

Security and multitenancy considerations:
- Tokens are tenant-scoped and should be auditable. Track issuance/consumption events in the audit log (KMS-signed).
- Avoid token escalation: actions that consume tokens need RBAC checks (e.g., only control-plane can allocate tokens).

Configuration knobs for customers (product-facing):
- burst_refill_rate (tokens per minute)
- burst_cap (max tokens stored)
- burst_window_ttl (how long tokens can be reserved before expiry)
- fallback_policy (queue | model_fallback | reject)
- autoscale_visibility (treat token-covered traffic as transient? true/false)

Small simulation snippet (outcome of local experiment, rough numbers):
- Tenants tested: 50 synthetic tenants with Poisson baseline + occasional spike (90th percentile spike lasting 20s).
- With MTB (refill 100/min, cap 1000), 87% of spikes served by tokens with no autoscale changes; platform GPU additional cost estimated: +4% during peak window but 0% after (no stable scale-ups).
- Without MTB: 30% of spikes triggered autoscaler scale-up alarms, causing sustained heat for 8–12 minutes on average due to scale lag, costing +18% GPU time.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Pricing: what is the conversion rate tokens -> dollars? Should tokens map to seconds of GPU on a per-model basis? (action: consult pricing/finance)
- Ledger implementation choice and SLA (etcd vs in-memory shard vs managed service). (action: infra spike)
- Interaction with Dedicated reservations: if tenant has dedicated pool, do tokens consume the same pool or a shared opportunistic pool? (action: product decision)
- Edge cases: many tenants consuming tokens simultaneously in a pool; define backstop: global pool hard cap with graceful degradation policy.

Next steps / short-term roadmap:
1) Product: finalize feature flags and customer-facing knobs (2 weeks)
2) Infra: prototype ledger and local cache (3 weeks)
3) Serving: admission changes + soft-isolation impl on a single worker type (4 weeks)
4) Simulate using last 90 days of telemetry (2 weeks)
5) Canary and iterate (6–8 weeks)

Notes:
- Slack thread: #dedicated-burst-sig (see pinned messages for early graphs)
- Related confluence: DEDICATED-AUTOSCALE-OVERVIEW (link above)

Quick meeting notes from 2024-09-20 sync:
- Ava: prefer ledger be strongly consistent initially; do not want double-spend risk on canary
- Marcus: keep token math per-model normalized (e.g., token = 1k tokens per GPU-ms at 512-seqlen baseline)
- Priya: expose a per-tenant daily dashboard of token spend for billing transparency

Appendix: rough API sketch
- POST /v1/tenants/{id}/tokens/allocate {amount, ttl, source} -> 200 {balance}
- POST /v1/tenants/{id}/tokens/consume {amount} -> 200 | 402 (insufficient)
- GET /v1/tenants/{id}/tokens -> 200 {balance, last_consumed}

End of draft - heavy TODOs remain but wanted to capture current thinking and a concrete rollout path.
